# Diabetic neuropathy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Disorders of glucose metabolism > Diabetic neuropathy*

[Original Article Link](/library/Nt0-d3)

---

## Summary

Diabetic neuropathy is a progressive nerve injury caused by chronic <u>hyperglycemia</u>. <u>Distal</u> symmetric <u>polyneuropathy</u> and <u>autonomic neuropathy</u> are the most common types; less common manifestations include mononeuropathy and <u>radiculopathy</u>. Patients with <u>distal</u> symmetric <u>polyneuropathy</u> typically present with sensory loss of the lower extremities and may also have motor <u>weakness</u>, although many affected individuals are asymptomatic. Diagnosis is typically clinical, and management includes glycemic control and daily foot care. Pharmacological therapy may be considered for <u>pain management</u>. In <u>diabetic autonomic neuropathy</u>, clinical presentation, recommended diagnostic studies, and treatment vary depending on the organ system involved. Annual <u>screening for diabetic neuropathy</u> is recommended for all patients with <u>diabetes</u>, starting at the time of diagnosis for patients with <u>type 2 diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>T2DM</u>) and 5 years after diagnosis for patients with <u>type 1 diabetes mellitus</u> (<u>T1DM</u>).




See also “<u>Diabetic gastroparesis</u>.”

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Diabetic polyneuropathy</u> is the most common form of <u>polyneuropathy</u> in high-income countries. [[2]](/library/9d1NHf0)[[3]](/library/G0WBhP0)

* ∼ 50% of patients with <u>diabetes</u> develop <u>peripheral neuropathy</u>. [[4]](/library/H0WKhP0)

* Up to 90% of patients with <u>diabetes</u> may develop <u>autonomic neuropathy</u>.  [[5]](/library/s0WthP0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

Chronic <u>hyperglycemia</u> causes <u>glycation</u> of <u>axon</u> <u>proteins</u> and subsequent development of progressive sensomotor neuropathy; typically affects multiple <u>peripheral nerves</u>.

---

## Diabetic peripheral neuropathy

* Frequently asymptomatic, but can lead to the development of additional diabetic complications (e.g., <u>diabetic foot</u>) [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)

* Types include: [[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)

* <u>Distal symmetric polyneuropathy in diabetes</u>

* A bilateral progressive neuropathy causing sensory loss and/or <u>pain</u> in a <u>stocking glove pattern</u>

* Most common form of diabetic neuropathy (75%)

* Mononeuropathy

* A focal neuropathy that affects a single nerve (e.g., <u>cranial</u> mononeuropathy, <u>mononeuropathy multiplex</u>)

* Affects < 10% of patients with <u>diabetic peripheral neuropathy</u> [[4]](/library/H0WKhP0)

* <u>Diabetic radioculoplexus neuropathy</u>: most commonly diabetic lumbosacral plexopathy, which manifests as thigh <u>pain</u> and <u>proximal</u> <u>muscle weakness</u>

* Treatment-induced neuropathy in diabetes (<u>insulin neuritis</u>): a rare small-fiber neuropathy triggered by an improvement in blood <u>glucose</u> levels after chronic <u>hyperglycemia</u>

---

## Clinical features

Many individuals with <u>diabetic peripheral neuropathy</u> are asymptomatic and the condition is often detected only during screening or after complications develop. [[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)[[8]](/library/f_1knj0)[[9]](/library/wV1h9f0)




* Sensory symptoms

* Common features

* <u>Distal</u> symmetrical sensory loss: <u>stocking glove sensory loss pattern</u> with <u>proximal</u> progression

* Numbness

* Tingling

* <u>Dysesthesia</u> (e.g., <u>burning feet syndrome</u> with symptoms that worsen at night)

* Less common features

* <u>Allodynia</u>

* <u>Hyperesthesia</u>

* Motor <u>weakness</u>: e.g., <u>ataxia</u>, balance issues

* <u>Neurological examination</u> may show loss or reduction of:

* <u>Ankle reflex</u>

* <u>Vibration sense</u> (using a tuning fork)

* <u>Sharp/dull discrimination</u> (e.g., <u>pinprick sensation</u>)

* <u>Light touch</u> (e.g., <u>monofilament test</u> )

* <u>Proprioception</u>

* <u>Temperature sensation</u>





> [!TIP]
> Approximately 50% of patients with <u>diabetic peripheral neuropathy</u> are asymptomatic. [[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)

## Management

* Manage underlying etiologies. [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)[[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)

* Optimize glycemic control (see “<u>Glycemic targets in diabetes</u>”).

* Treat <u>dyslipidemia</u> and <u>hypertension</u>, if present.

* See “<u>Management of hypercholesterolemia</u>.”

* See “<u>Hypertension management</u>.”

* Educate patients and caregivers on measures to prevent complications (e.g., <u>preventive measures against diabetic foot</u>). [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)

* Provide <u>pain</u> relief if necessary (see “<u>Analgesia for peripheral neuropathy</u>”).

* First-line medications include <u>pregabalin</u>, <u>duloxetine</u>, <u>venlafaxine</u>, and <u>amitriptyline</u>. [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)

* Follow up with patients regularly; adjust medication if <u>pain</u> remains inadequately controlled after 12 weeks of use. [[10]](/library/Ye1nxf0)

* For patients with severe or refractory symptoms, consider referral to a <u>pain management</u> specialist.

* Refer to <u>neurology</u> in case of diagnostic uncertainty.





> [!TIP]
> Good glycemic control can prevent the onset and progression of diabetic neuropathy, but it cannot reverse existing nerve damage. [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)

---

## Complications

* <u>Diabetic foot</u> <u>ulcers</u>

* <u>Diabetic neuropathic arthropathy</u> (<u>Charcot foot</u>)

* See also “<u>Diabetic foot</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Diabetic neuropathy is a major <u>risk factor</u> for <u>diabetic foot ulcers</u>. [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)

## Clinical features

### Genitourinary <u>autonomic neuropathy</u> [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)




* <u>Sexual dysfunction</u> (e.g., <u>erectile dysfunction</u>)

* <u>Neurogenic bladder</u>, e.g.:

* <u>Urinary retention</u>

* Incomplete <u>bladder</u> emptying

* <u>Bladder</u> distention

* <u>Overflow incontinence</u>

* Poor urinary stream





### Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)




* Early: decreased <u>heart</u> variability [[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)

* Late:

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u> at rest





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy</u> are at increased risk for silent <u>myocardial infarction</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u>, and <u>death</u>. [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)[[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)




### Gastrointestinal <u>autonomic neuropathy</u> [[6]](/library/0_1e5j0)




* <u>Diabetic gastroparesis</u>

* Stool changes (e.g., <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>fecal incontinence</u>, <u>constipation</u>)

* <u>Esophageal dysmotility</u>





### Other <u>autonomic neuropathies</u> [[7]](/library/ae1Qxf0)




* Impaired <u>pupillary</u> tone  [[11]](/library/gc1Fbf0)

* Sudomotor dysfuncton

* Dry <u>skin</u>

* Heat intolerance

* Abnormal sweating (e.g., <u>anhidrosis</u>, <u>gustatory sweating</u>)

* <u>Hypoglycemia unawareness</u>
